subsubtopic: REASON FOR DELAY IN ACTING TO AVOID POSSIBLE OIL SPILL FROM "KURDISTAN"-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of some urgency to Canadians.
Given the presence of two actual and one potential environmentally dangerous hazards arising out of the Kurdistan incident, and in view of accessible, dedicated, knowledgeable and highly competent professional advice, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay):
That this House call on the Minister of Transport, the Minister of the Environment, and the Deputy Prime Minister to explain on motions later today why it took up to six days to decide on a course of action with respect to the stern section, and on the Prime Minister of the country to explain why the Nova Scotia government was not fully consulted in the decision-making process.

REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON "KURDISTAN" INCIDENT-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43 refers to the same subject matter. It relates to the shipping and environmental policies and methods of this government in the matter of the Kurdistan which, as the House knows, is an oil tanker in distress off Chedabucto Bay.
Since this vessel, with her engine-room sound and intact and steam in her boilers, could, as so many crippled vessels in the past, have proceeded under her own power or with minimal assistance to a suitable port; and since the Minister of Transport, who had ultimate authority, delayed and dithered for several days while drift ice closed in and complicated matters, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall):
That the minister or his acting minister, today on motions, make a statement setting out the reasons for the indecisiveness and confusion which has paralysed this government, years after the Arrow disaster in the same area underscored the necessity for coherent plans, legislative authority and automatic decision-making powers to act expeditiously in matters such as this, and to assure the House, Mr. Speaker, that under the guidance of the Minister of Transport, the Kurdistan is not making due progress toward Cerebus Rock for a repeat performance.

subsubtopic: TIMING OF DECISION TO SALVAGE OIL TANKER "KURDISTAN"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. It is now nine years since the Arrow disaster in the Strait of Canso

March 23, 1979
Oral Questions
off the Nova Scotia coast. I have two or three questions I would like to direct to the minister. Precisely when in time were the minister's advisers able to determine the integrity of the hull and the engine-room of the oil tanker Kurdistan and decide that it could be salvaged in a reasonably safe operation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: TIMING OF DECISION TO SALVAGE OIL TANKER "KURDISTAN"
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as soon as it was possible to investigate the stern section, that fact was ascertained. I cannot tell the hon. member when they reached the conclusion that it was indeed safe. I was first given a preliminary indication of that in a briefing three mornings ago. At that stage, further examination was still going to take place. I am interested in finding out why the hon. member is interested in exactly what happened at what stage of the process.

subsubtopic: TIMING OF DECISION TO SALVAGE OIL TANKER "KURDISTAN"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, six days is too long to gamble on an environmental hazard created by the wiles of the ice-packs in the Cabot Strait and the Gulf of St. Lawrence, and the weather, particularly at this time of year.
Why did the government have to wait? Why could it not deal with the legal problems with more dispatch? Is it because neither the minister's department nor the Department of the Environment have adequate statutory authority to deal with matters of this nature with much greater dispatch? Was it a technical, or a legal problem that caused the undue delay?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: TIMING OF DECISION TO SALVAGE OIL TANKER "KURDISTAN"
speechtext:
It was a combination of things, Mr. Speaker; but I do not grant for a moment that there was undue delay. It was a very serious decision to take, to allow a vessel which had suffered any kind of mishap to come alongside the Canadian coastline with a cargo of oil on board.
We wanted to be sure on the technical basis that the risk was small. We also wanted to have complete protection from a legal point of view in relation to any possible costs and damage even though it was small. Experts in relation to this kind of contract came together from quite a few different places in the world, experts who had been associated with a similar event in Rotterdam and the like.
The question of negotiation and the extent of liability which we would insist upon were important questions on which I wanted to be satisfied. In the meantime, however, it was not as though the time was being lost. The vessel was put under tow. At first, while there was a question about the adequacy of the stern to survive the seas, it was being moved in an outward direction toward deeper water. When it became apparent that salvage was distinctly possible, and having regard to winds in any case, the direction of the tow was changed: it moved toward the Port Hawkesbury destination. When the critical point was reached where it would have been necessary to turn either out to the sea or in toward the bay, the decision had already been made.
Therefore, while the legal matters did take some time, it was not as though time was lost. I hope the hon. member will agree with us that in making a most serious decision involving an

element of risk it was necessary to be sure as to the size of that risk and be completely protected from the legal and financial points of view.

subsubtopic: TIMING OF DECISION TO SALVAGE OIL TANKER "KURDISTAN"
speechtext:
The minister's response is totally inadequate, of course. Six days is far too long to gamble on ice and weather conditions in the Guif of St. Lawrence, and the minister knows it.
May I direct a final question to the Acting Prime Minister, whoever he may be today, and ask whether in his view it would be worth while, once the formal investigation into this matter has been completed, to refer this whole question to an appropriate standing committee of the House in order to determine whether the existing statutory authority available to the Minister of Transport and to the Minister of State for the Eviron-ment is adequate to enable them to cope with disasters of this nature with much more dispatch than we have seen in the last week?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: TIMING OF DECISION TO SALVAGE OIL TANKER "KURDISTAN"
speechtext:
Obviously, in the course of examining the alternatives available to us we have begun to draw some conclusions about our powers and the exact legal situation in a variety of very difficult circumstances. I would think that, as a result, we would be coming forward in due course with some changes.
I do not think we needed a different set of powers in the situation which actually faced us, but as we reviewed alternative circumstances, when we were not sure what those circumstances would be, I was concerned about the extent of our powers and I will want to propose some legislative changes.

subtopic: ICE SURVEILLANCE CAPABILITY IN GULF OF ST. LAWRENCE

speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subtopic: ICE SURVEILLANCE CAPABILITY IN GULF OF ST. LAWRENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wonder if I might direct some supplementary questions to the born-again Minister of Transport. The same ice conditions that are compounding the threat to the tanker Kurdistan have caused the entire CN ferry fleet to be stuck in the Gulf of St. Lawrence, with 317 passengers stranded on three ships. A fourth, the Frederick Carter, left port this morning only to be caught in the ice a short time later.
Where is our ice surveillance capability? Why would these ships leave port, knowing that the wind has not changed, knowing full well they will be stuck in the ice, knowing full well we do not have the ice-breaking capacity to free them? Why would the coastguard allow this to happen?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: ICE SURVEILLANCE CAPABILITY IN GULF OF ST. LAWRENCE
speechtext:
Essentially, I think, because of the hope in each case that the trip might be completed. A good deal of our ice-breaker strength is, of course, in the vicinity. These vessels are helping in every way they can. Obviously, there are people waiting to board the ferries, and if there is any chance at all I am sure they move out.
I have not inquired into the exact circumstances of the departure of each vessel, which is probably what the hon. member has in mind. After all, this involves a judgment by
March 23, 1979

local management and those who operate the vessels, no doubt in response to the needs of people who want to make the crossing.

subtopic: ICE SURVEILLANCE CAPABILITY IN GULF OF ST. LAWRENCE
speechtext:
I am astounded at the minister's reply. One of these ships, the Robert Bond, with 60 passengers aboard, has been stuck in the ice since 2 o'clock last Monday. Surely the Canadian coastguard has some jurisdiction. Surely it must have weather data at its disposal; it must have knowledge of ice conditions. After all, ice is not unknown in the Cabot Strait at this time of year: perhaps the minister does not know that.
Why has this situation been allowed to arise? Why has it been allowed to get worse, with people stranded at Port aux Basques and Sydney, with another ferry leaving this morning? Surely the coastguard must have some jurisdiction here and, if not, why not?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: ICE SURVEILLANCE CAPABILITY IN GULF OF ST. LAWRENCE
speechtext:
The coastguard is certainly in operation in connection with this exercise. The Labrador and the St. Laurent are there, hard at work in an effort to free these vessels. 1 cannot understand the hon. member's logic. He is critical of the fact that passengers are stranded at Sydney and Port aux Basques. At the same time he is critical of the fact that vessels move out when we should know that at this time of year there is ice in the strait. Is he suggesting that we cancel service cross the strait at certain times of the year because there may be ice? I think that is a rather ridiculous suggestion.
I suggest that the right thing is to rely on the judgment of the people who are operating the vessels and who expect that, with coastguard help, they may be able to get through. When, suddenly, very difficult winds trap vessels which are ordinarily capable of managing the ice, obviously there is a difficulty. But I do not think the hon. member has any solution, unless he wants to build airports at each end as well.

subtopic: ICE SURVEILLANCE CAPABILITY IN GULF OF ST. LAWRENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are not dealing with a hypothetical situation; we are dealing with ice which has been there since last Monday. One ferry has been stuck since last Monday, yet CN continues to accept passengers, knowing the weather has not changed and knowing ice conditions are still the same. Ships are still allowed to leave the port, knowing full well that a short while after leaving either Port aux Basques or Sydney they will be caught in the ice.
What does the minister intend to do about it? Does he intend to put in place some kind of ice surveillance capability which would say to CN, "Sorry, you cannot leave today because the ice has packed in, the wind is not changing and you are going to be stuck"? Why does the Canadian coastguard not provide that kind of service?

subsubtopic: THREAT OF OIL POLLUTION TO FISHERY AND BEACHES IN TOWING "KURDISTAN"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Minister of State (Environment) and it relates to the Kurdistan incident.
In view of the concern expressed by fishermen in the Canso Strait area that the federal government has allowed the stern section of the oil tanker Kurdistan to be towed towards Chedabucto Bay, and given the discovery of a new oil slick in the area, can the minister explain why the towing commenced, given the dangerous ice conditions in the bay and the real threat of pollution on the beaches and in the fishing grounds? Many of us fear that the value of the cargo is taking precedence over safety of the environment.

subsubtopic: THREAT OF OIL POLLUTION TO FISHERY AND BEACHES IN TOWING "KURDISTAN"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, environmentally, all factors were evaluated. A number of other ports were evaluated as well. In the view of my officials who are on the scene, as well as in the view of Environment Nova Scotia, the Department of Fisheries and the Department of Transport, the route to Port Hawkesbury, with all of the conditions which the salvor would have to agree to, was the safest one to take.
It was the view of our officials that with the appropriate icebreaking equipment on hand, there really was no environmental risk or, at least, that the risk if any was really very minimal.

subsubtopic: THREAT OF OIL POLLUTION TO FISHERY AND BEACHES IN TOWING "KURDISTAN"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in light of that answer, I wonder if the minister can explain reports in the media this morning that the plans to tow the tanker to Port Hawkesbury have been abandoned because officials of the oil industry say it is too dangerous to move it through the dangerous ice conditions in the bay for unloading at Hawkesbury. I would like the minister to inform the House whether this is true or not.
In addition, given the past experience of the Arrow oil spill disaster, can the minister explain why it has taken so long- over six days-to determine what course of action to take? It seems to me that this is an indication that the government is not well prepared.

March 23, 1979
Oral Questions

subsubtopic: THREAT OF OIL POLLUTION TO FISHERY AND BEACHES IN TOWING "KURDISTAN"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am checking on the validity of those press reports. It is my understanding that all appropriate arrangements have been made for the stern once it arrives at Port Hawkesbury. I think my colleague, the Minister of Transport, explained very clearly, in an answer he gave earlier to the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East, why it took six days. Those six days were not all lost by doing nothing. It took some time for both the stern and the bow sections to be in a position which would allow a decision to be made.
If the hon. member will recall, the weather conditions were absolutely awful in the whole area and a lot of danger was involved. If the decision had been taken to tow the vessel into deep water, they would have been bucking severe weather conditions. There is a possibility it could not have been done, two lines could have broken, and so on. So the decision was made that the best possible solution was to attach tugs to both the stern and the bow sections and try to nurse them along in the best way possible until a decision was made. Now a decision has been made and we are just waiting for the fog to clear at Chedabucto Bay so that the stern can be brought safely into Port Hawkesbury.

subsubtopic: THREAT OF OIL POLLUTION TO FISHERY AND BEACHES IN TOWING "KURDISTAN"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, again I worry about the safety aspects, since the reports say that a new oil slick has been sighted. If the government intends to proceed to tow the stern into the bay, then indeed the fishery may be in danger.
My final supplementary is this: The minister says that all the legal ramifications and the insurance problems explain the six-day delay in coming to a decision as to which way to tow the stern. Surely the minister would agree that, in light of the Arrow incident, his department should have had regulations in place so there would not be this delay in terms of determining liability and what the insurance results would be.

subsubtopic: THREAT OF OIL POLLUTION TO FISHERY AND BEACHES IN TOWING "KURDISTAN"
speechtext:
I do not think there was really any serious delay. As far as the advice being given by my officials is concerned, it had nothing to do with the legalities: these were being negotiated by Transport Canada. The advice that my officials gave was based on environmental grounds and we agreed finally with the decision, which was agreed to by all parties concerned, that the safest thing to do environmentally was to go into Port Hawkesbury.
I would say to the hon. member that there has been some oil-stained ice observed in the vicinity, or north of the entrance to Chedabucto Bay. It is oil-stained floe ice which we feel came into that area from the original site where the tanker Kurdistan broke up. We do not have a complete evaluation of it yet, but since we found it yesterday there have been a number of surveillance flights over it. To the best of our knowledge, there is really no danger at this point. This is not a slick; the officials are calling it oil-stained ice. There is no environmental danger observed. But we hope we will be able to get people on site and not just rely on aerial observations. We will be able to bring people on site today to observe exactly the condition of these oil stains, and if any clean-up action has to

be taken, we have plans and equipment and it will be taken once we have made the evaluation.

Poverty is such in Canada even today that we are trying to pay a supplement to those Canadians who are the most

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask another supplementary.
In view of the study conducted by the health and welfare department on the establishment of a national guaranteed minimum income scheme, reports of which were distributed to members, does the minister intend to pursue this line in order to achieve these objectives which would, in my view, help fight poverty? I am thinking only of the national level, disregarding the position of the provinces in this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER GOVERNMENT WILL CONTRIBUTE TO ESTABLISHMENT IN QUEBEC OF GUARANTEED ANNUAL INCOME
speechtext: It is very difficult in the present climate of economic restraint in Canada and in each of the provinces to speak of a universal guaranteed annual income scheme- which would be the ideal-unilaterally funded by the federal government, for the simple reason that it would cost $7 billion. I have just received estimates in this regard. However, it is possible to implement selective programs aimed at the most vulnerable and needy groups, such as children living in poverty, and that is why we will continue to adopt such measures as the child tax credit.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the very nimble Minister of Finance and the Acting Prime Minister. It concerns the extraordinarily complacement remarks made yesterday that the rate of inflation is a little high. With, now, five years since the last election and with the rate of inflation running at about 9 per cent annually, I ask the minister what has happened to the fiery desire of his leader to wrestle inflation to the ground?
What has happened to the assurances given by the government some four years ago that by now we would have a rate of inflation of 4 per cent? Why is the Minister of Finance now almost accepting the current rate of inflation and saying that it is a little high?

subsubtopic: ATTITUDE OF GOVERNMENT TO HIGH RATE OF INFLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we do not accept the fact that inflation is at a normal level. We are trying to reduce it as quickly and as effectively as possible. Despite the decline of the Canadian dollar in relation to the American dollar, our rate of inflation is lower than that of the United States. However, I do find that it is too high. I would like to reduce it, and I have made predictions that the rate of inflation will be declining to the end of the year.
Most economic spokesmen say that inflation will go down during the year but not as low as everyone would like to see it. Everyone would like to have a zero rate of inflation. It seems to me that because of world conditions at this time, and with increases in the price of oil and other pressures coming not only from internal sources but from external sources, it will be very difficult to reach the goal we have in mind and achieve a very low rate or even a zero rate of inflation. I am quite sure that by the end of the year inflation in Canada will be lower than it is today.

subsubtopic: ATTITUDE OF GOVERNMENT TO HIGH RATE OF INFLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have had a succession of assurances and predictions from successive ministers of finance, yet what we have is a state of affairs where the rate of inflation is around 9 per cent and Canadians are now borrowing money to maintain their standard of living.
Does the Minister of Finance and his colleagues say nothing more than "Zap; you are frozen at a rate of inflation of 8 to 9 per cent"?

subsubtopic: ATTITUDE OF GOVERNMENT TO HIGH RATE OF INFLATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, we said that we are having a problem with inflation. We decided to go back to the marketplace. It is a problem that is afflicting not only Canada but everybody else. It would be unrealistic for anyone to say that we can cure inflation just by wishing that inflation would go away.
I have said many times that Canadians over the last year have shown a lot of responsibility; that we have regained our competitive position in world markets and that the competitive level in Canada is such that the increase in unit costs is lower

than that in the United States. We have extended our external markets and we put 400,000 Canadians back to work in the last year. Despite the fact that the Canadian dollar is weaker than it was a year ago, the inflation rate is lower in Canada than it is in the United States. That is not a bad performance.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. The parliamentary secretary was doing so well; he answered six questions just yesterday, which was incredible. Now all of a sudden the number is reduced to three. At this speed we would be here for another two years before all the questions on the order paper are answered.

The House resumed, from Thursday, March 22, consideration of the motion of Mr. Gillespie (for the Minister of Finance) that Bill C-38, to amend the Excise Tax Act, be read the second time and referred to a committee of the whole.

Mr. Speaker, I take pleasure in being able to participate in this debate on Bill C-38, to amend Canada's excise taxes. I might say that it does seem a little late in coming. The Liberal government has always prided itself on being good administrators of the economy and of matters in the House. Nevertheless the budget speech from which this bill emanates was made November 16. It is now March 23 and we have just started debate on the bill. That is a period of four months between introduction of the bill and debate and is a sad commentary on the way the government has managed House business. It is the power of positive failure. I think the people of Canada are catching on to this attitude.
Bill C-38 does three main things. It revises the airline tax, the gas tax and the sales tax in some complicated jargon. I will comment on some of the amendments which the government has made.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) has been quite vocal in the House, in fact laudatory, of his policy of making users pay. The bill before us increases the airline travel tax from $8 to $15. This is almost a 100 per cent increase. It seems to me that the government has again been guilty of some bad management. Not only has it over-built some airports, but it has faced some very high cost overruns in the contruction of those airports. Other hon. members and myself have mentioned the cost of overruns associated with the Calgary airport and Mirabel airport. The construction costs for Calgary International Airport escalated from $57 million to $127 million, more than double the amount of the original estimates.
The Auditor General said at page 506 of his report:
The air carriers expressed strong reservations as to the immediate need for, and concern about the cost of, new terminal facilities.
It is one thing to have a user-pay policy, but it is another thing to make the users prisoners of government policy. It would be all right if users had a choice between that method of transportation and another method. I could then see the rationale for the Minister of Transport's policy of user-pay. However, in a country like ours where air transport is becoming increasingly important and perhaps even mandatory if Canadian citizens wish to see the country and carry on business, for the government to construct facilities which the airlines did not want in the first place and for which users of airlines must pay-because of the Minister of Transport's policy-is making people prisoners of a taxation system from which they cannot get out. If people had an alternative it

March 23, 1979
Excise Tax Act
would be another matter, but many of us do not have that opportunity.
Again I mention the construction costs of the Mirabel airport which escalated to the fine tune of S600 million. It strikes me as somewhat ludicrous that the government continually wants to justify the construction of that airport. I now find that when you fly Air Canada from Ottawa to Europe, instead of going to Mirabel which is 100 miles away, you go to Toronto which is 300 miles away. Obviously Air Canada is not crazy about the idea of using Mirabel even though we have this $600 million bill before us plus $1 million a week operating costs.
The government was not able to explain that not only was it costly to over-build the airport, but there would be the additional cost of operating that airport. Now the Minister of Transport through the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) wants to apply the user-pay philosophy so that the public who are now obligated to use those facilities have to pay twice.
The hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) made some very useful observations in his speech yesterday. I simply want to repeat some of them. I quote from page 4431 of Hansard:
I have a breakdown of the cost of landing a Boeing 747 in Toronto. These figures are based on October 1, 1978, data. I put these figures on the record so hon. members can be apprised of what it costs to land a jumbo jet. The particular example I will give is of a transoceanic flight with a full passenger load. The costs include the en route North Atlantic fee in the amount of $130; the landing fee amounting to $1,596; the general terminal fee assessed at $267; security charge for 429 passengers at 20 cents per passenger amounting to $86; and the fuel throughput charge for 22,000 gallons at 1.5 cents per gallon, amounting to $330. Then we have a provincial fuel tax on 22,000 gallons at three cents per gallon, which amounts to $660, and a transportation tax, 429 passengers at $8, which amounts to $3,432. When you total all those together, and it does not take into consideration the rental of the airline space for counters and so on, it works out to $6,501 to land a 747 with 429 passengers aboard. Those are the rates effective October 1, 1978.
The impact of the transportation tax at $15 per person will change that $3,432 figure to $6,435. The immediate 30 per cent increase which is going to be imposed on an annual basis over an eight year period when these new landing fees are going to be implemented, will increase that $6,500 figure to $9,604. Those are the kinds of increases about which we are talking.
It costs the airline passenger more to travel. He not only has to pay the extra $7 for the privilege of using the airport facilities, but the extra landing fees. The figures presented to us yesterday by the hon. member for Vegreville do not include the cost of purchasing and maintaining the aircraft and paying the cabin crew and ground crew. Because the minister has over-built the air terminals and because those overbuilt air terminals cost more to maintain-
And the aborted ones like Pickering.

As the hon. member for Vegreville says, and the aborted ones like Pickering. All those costs are written into the extravagances of this government. Now the minister wants user-pay. Frankly, the passengers have been used. It is no longer user-pay; it is the used who have to pay.

The bill also deals with gasoline tax. I remember the time about four years ago when we increased the tax on gasoline to be paid to the federal government to ten cents a gallon. The then ministers of finance, two ministers ago, said that much of that tax would ensure conservation of our oil reserves. The excise tax on light aircraft and outboard engines was being imposed in order to help conservation.
Now we have an entirely new tack. Parenthetically, we worried at that time about the government policy that the ten cent tax would be refundable to businesses, fishermen, logging companies, farmers and so forth. We wondered how much of a bureaucracy that would involve, how many people would be hired to count the receipts submitted by those people, how many people would be required in national revenue to tally the receipts and make sure the deductions are legitimate.
Members receive a lot of representations asking why the tax is ten cents a gallon. Rather than increase the tax ten cents a gallon for a few, why not make it five cents a gallon for everyone and cut out a lot of the bureaucracy? Again the government does not pay attention. The argument is conservation; we are going to save energy.
Clause 14 includes a schedule which indicates a special imposition for those with cars that use non-leaded gas. I thought the additional gadgets on these cars were to be pollution control devices. Canadians were encouraged to purchase cars which use that kind of gas. In clause 14 there is a new category, and I quote:
1. Petroleum products, namely,
(a)	gasoline, premium, no lead	1.3 cents per litre;(b)	gasoline, grade 1	1.2 cents per litre;(c)	gasoline, grade 2	1.1 cents per litre;(d)	gasoline, no lead	1.1 cents per litre;(e) diesel fuel	1.0 cents per litre;-
The government says it wants to encourage economy. It wants to encourage the use of anti-pollution devices on automobiles and then taxes those who co-operate with the government. I wish to quote from a letter I received from a constituent dated February 14, before this tax was added:
Why is it that the person who operates a pollution controlled vehicle has to pay more for his gas? Don't you think the users of regular grade gas should pay the shot for polluting the atmosphere? I see no great problem for the government to reverse the tax to encourage the use of pollution controlled vehicles. If this is not done soon I will remove the controls from my vehicle so that I too can enjoy cheaper driving. I know that the gas companies claim that the higher price is to pay for new equipment, so it is up to the government to make the ones who are doing the polluting pay for this lopsided public nuisance. I would like some kind of an answer on this subject.
Although I have written to the minister, I do not expect an answer that will satisfy my constituent or myself. Last week I spoke to another constituent who had just come from the garage after having the anti-pollution devices dismantled on her car in order to be able to use regular gas.
People who purchase cars that use unleaded gas which is required for the anti-pollution devices are being punished three times. First, they have to pay more for the car. They have to pay more when they buy a new car. I suppose they have to pay more for servicing, too, because of all the extra gadgets on it;
March 23, 1979

and now they have to pay more for the gas they use. The minister of the environment is calling for a reduction in pollution. Mr. Speaker, the minister of the environment has an office in those new buildings in Hull and his department is pumping raw sewage every day into the Ottawa River.
Shame!
That is the kind of leadership we get from this government. Here, in the bill before us, unleaded gas costs more, by reason of a tax, than other gas.
Read subsection (d).

I did. That applies to unleaded, unregular gas, but if you use a premium gas you pay more tax on it than on any of the other classes. I believe the government needs to readjust its vision with regard to these matters although I have little hope of that happening.
When the Minister of Finance made his speech last November, he said, among other things:
In my view, the special 10 per cent excise tax on marine engines and private aircraft and the 5 per cent tax on motorcycles are having adverse economic effects. The contribution of these taxes to energy conservation has been minimal.
I guess that jargon is the minister's way of saying the tax did not work. I wish he had put it as plainly as that. He probably could not police the application of the tax-he had no way of collecting it properly. He could not handle the administration.
I have one final comment and it relates to the reduction of the sales tax from 12 per cent to 9 per cent. Again, this was a good idea badly handled. As the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Malone) told us last night, one automobile dealer in his riding said he was able to handle it because he had two sets of cars on his lot: one part of the inventory he had bought before the tax reduction was introduced and the other part consisted of cars he had bought afterwards. So there were different prices on what were virtually the same cars. He bailed out of it at the cost of SI2,000 to the business and I suppose his loss will be deductible as a business expense.
But what about the customers who suffered? What about the loss of sales? Since the government took so long to bring down a budget in the first place, and since it has taken so long to bring down the resulting legislation, surely administrative changes could have been made so that the car dealers, the furniture dealers and businessmen across Canada could derive a decent advantage from the decision made by the minister and not be punished for the government's bad management.
I do not expect many answers to these questions from the government side. After all, they have not been forthcoming in months past and I do not look for any help from them this time. At a time when they are trying to bail themselves out before an election, I look for more band-aids; I do not expect any solutions.
Excise Tax Act

Mr. Speaker, I should like to take a few minutes to state my views on that famous Bill C-38, and Act to amend the Excise Tax Act. This bill would implement the excise tax ways and means motions tabled in the House by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) on November 16 and on January 25 last. This bill would implement the terms of the budget affecting in one way or another the Excise Tax Act. However the bill does not particularly affect Quebeckers and Canadians. For that reason, I do not wish to spend too much time analysing that legislation. I will therefore criticize the bill while explaining the legislation at the same time.
In the first place, the provisions deal with the transportation of an individual by air. The government wishes to increase the tax it collects on the price of tickets from passengers travelling in the taxation area, that is in the North American zone, including the United States, except Hawaii, Canada and the Miquelon Islands. The tax would be raised from 8 to 15 per cent, the ceiling being $15 instead of the current limit of $8.
The tax levied on international trips was to go up from $8 to $12 during an undetermined period of time before reaching the ceiling of $15. However, the government has elected to combine both phases in one single operation. The purpose of that tax is to make users of those services pay for maintenance costs of national airports. The government thus hopes to increase its revenue by more that $72 million for the 1979-80 taxation year. Such a step is surely advisable, but before triumphing we should make sure what is the percentage of the cost effectively paid by users.
In addition, the government is amending clause 21 in Part III of the legislation dealing with the excise tax on cosmetics, jewellery, radio sets, etc. Thus, it is proposed to increase the tax on gasoline for cars as it is delivered at the service station, whether it is operated by the producer or somebody else. The gasoline is normally taxed when delivered by the producer to the independent retailer. However, when the producer also operates the service station, the legislation now provides that the payment can be deferred until the gasoline is sold to consumers.
The new legislation will therefore streamline the procedure. The government also proposes that persons seeking repayment of the special excise tax on gasoline or the federal sales tax on taxable items are entitled to the same scheme as taxpayers who are permit holders under the act. Because of this change, any person making a false statement for the purpose of obtaining repayment or failing to reimburse any overpayment, would be liable to the same penalty as any taxpayer who holds a permit as a retailer in similar circumstances.
The purpose of the third subclause is to provide for an excise tax exemption in the case of gasoline or aviation gasoline
4458

Excise Tax Act
which is sold to a person to whom a bulk permit has been issued for use by this person. When the holder of such a permit uses these privileges for purposes other than those described in this subclause, the permit holder must pay the special tax as any other taxpayer. Bill C-38 deals with the general reduction of the sales tax imposed on all manufacturers by the Canadian government. As hon. members doubtless know, this tax imposed on November 16, 1978, was lowered from 12 to 9 per cent on all goods sold by manufacturers and wholesalers who are permit holders and on all imported goods.
Clause 4 confirms these policies. Elowever, the government maintains the 12 per cent sales tax on imported and domestic wines. The purpose of subclauses 2 and 3 is to provide that the consumption or sales tax in the case of goods produced or manufactured in Canada for use by the producer or manufacturer be payable at the time the goods are used or appropriated for use.
We could state again here the opposition our party made to the reduction of the federal sales tax during the debate on the budget in November of last year. As a matter of fact, the reduction which the government proposed was only 3 per cent, while our own party proposed the complete elimination of the federal tax. What is more, since foodstuffs are goods of primary necessity, the consumer should benefit from a full exemption of the sales tax, so that have-nots may eat better for less money.
In Bill C-38, there is a tax of only 5 per cent imposed on food. It states that the governor in council. . . and I quote:
-may make regulations exemption any class of small manufacturer or producer from payment of consumption or sales tax on goods manufactured or produced-
The purpose of this amendment is to exclude from these benefits all firms which are not provided for under this clause, including larger corporations which publish printed matters for their own use, so that they may not be eligible for the exemption on their printed matters, unless the value of such printed matters is great enough to warrant an application for a licence.
Once again I see in that bill an invitation to favoritism since the department staff will determine what groups can benefit from the tax exemption on gasoline and aviation gasoline. How easy, what a splendid opportunity for bribes, Mr. Speaker! In addition, tax reimbursements resulting from the Tariff Board decisions cannot be made until the year after the taxes were paid. At the present time taxes are simply carried over to the following year. The new act would extend the reimbursement period to a four-year period. In fact, clause 9 would change clause 8 mentioned above and apply to any reimbursement of the special excise tax on gasoline or the federal sales tax on all taxable goods. Clause 10, Mr. Speaker, stipulates what penalties are incurred by whoever does not respect the provisions of the act. Finally, the Excise Tax Act is amended by cancelling the special tax of 5 per cent on big motorcycles and the special

tax of 10 per cent on marine motors of over 20HPs and aircraft belonging to individuals or companies.
Repeal of sections 10 and 12 of schedule I cancels the excise tax on those items. That tax had been justified by invoking the energy crisis. Today, when the government passes Bill C-42 to conserve energy, to allot oil supplies, it cancels the special tax on luxury cars that burn a lot of fuel. That attitude proves again the lack of planning this government has shown ever since it came to power. The other clause amends section 12.1 of schedule I of the present act, to take metric measures into account. In addition, clause 13 proposes that some consumer goods be completely exempt from the consumption or sales tax, such as solar water heaters and devices designed to convert sound to light signals for use by the deaf in telephones, door bells, timers for stoves and other similar goods. This last measure will give the deaf greater access to the technologies that can allow them to lead more normal lives despite their handicap. It also exempts from this federal tax all thermal insulation. Thermal material and rolls will continue to benefit from the exemption provided they meet the requirement of a thermal coefficient that is superior to 2.4 per inch.
The exemption on thermal insulation materials would be allowed only if the sheets or boards had a total thermal resistance of not less than 3. This clause abolishes the special provision for hard-sided trailers which were taxed on only 75 per cent of their selling price, which meant that the rate of the federal sales tax was actually 9 per cent. Therefore, the government acted dishonestly in leading Canadians to think that the general reduction of the federal or consumer sales tax to 9 per cent would allow this exemption to continue. However, we cannot take it for granted that the manufacturer will pass on to consumers this 3 per cent reduction. It has indeed been shown on several occasions that the federal sales tax reduction is only partially passed on to consumers wishing to buy a hard-side trailer. The government is thereby increasing the housing costs of people who often purchase these types of homes because they cannot afford a single family dwelling. This policy could be detrimental to some Canadians. Through this clause, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) is putting an end to the federal sales tax exemption on double windows, double doors and other such items. The government says: "Since glass is not as efficient for energy conservation as walls, the exemption has not achieved the aim initially envisaged."
Is the minister encouraging Canadians to build homes without doors or windows, because such things increase the loss of energy from dwellings? Schedule IV of the bill contains a chart on metric equivalents which must be respected to convert Imperial measures into European measures. It gives the excise tax on Imperial and metric measures of gas.
Finally, a clause gives the governor in council the right to simply repeal by order part II of the bill if he deems it
March 23, 1979

obsolete. No matter what kind of legislation is passed and accepted by parliament, it is always the minister who has the final word. It is called the governor in council, but in fact it is the minister who decides. If he decides in his great wisdom to simply repeal the legislation passed by parliament, that is up to him, and there is a clause protecting him. That is indeed provided for in all bills. That is why I often say that there is no use debating a bill for a week, two weeks, a month, two months, when we know in advance that two or three weeks after the minister can stop or restrict the application of the legislation. Clause 17 explains the procedures the members must go through in order to review the order made under the preceeding clause.
The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) explained during his speech last Monday that the practice adopted by the government whereby it introduces regulations greatly restricts the debates following the tabling of the order abrogating this amendment to the Excise Tax Act. Since we do not know now when the government will withdraw the legislation that it hopes to pass today, why does it want to restrict uselessly and illogically the length of a future debate? The hon. member for Edmonton West concluded his speech in the House by saying:
Here is another closure motion. Are we going to get this as a regular practice in every bill, that it will be provided that there shall be a motion for some consideration by parliament, that parliament will be able to debate that motion for three, five, ten or 20 hours, and then it will be brought to an end? What an easy way out for a government to take. We will be told ahead of time, by statute, how long parliament shall debate any question.
In view of this statement made by the hon. member, I would simply like to say that when we pass legislation according to the procedure followed by this parliament, we always wonder how long this legislation will last before senior officials decide that it is no longer useful. Mr. Speaker, I believe that when the government wants to make important changes, it should simply have to come before parliament and ask that clauses giving the government authority over parliament be withdrawn. This is something that I have never been able to accept.
Once again, we are considering a bill which will give supreme authority to senior officials since we all know that they are the ones who control all the actions of parliament. This is understandable since a minister who has just been appointed to a department certainly does not have the knowledge required if he does not have the help of his officials to compare all the legislation affecting his department. Moreover, I believe that it would be difficult to ask a minister to tell his officials what to do. Most often, it is the officials who tell the minister what to do. This is why I say that, finally, when we abrogate legislation passed by the government, it is the senior officials who have decided in all their wisdom that it was time to abrogate this legislation or to amend it according to their wishes.
When we see departmental officials acting like this, we always say: It is for the good of the citizens! It will create jobs!

However, since these decisions are made by senior officials, their interest lies in creating jobs in the public service to increase their army. This is why in the last several years we have seen government expenditures soaring to 41 per cent of the gross national product when we know that for many years the GNP has increased on the average by 4 per cent a year.
In addition to that increase, we still have to pay for more civil servants, 41 per cent of that same increased product. Then, Mr. Speaker, you no longer wonder why it costs so much to administer this country. Why does it cost so much? Because we have too many unproductive jobs, and I have always said in this House and I maintain that productive jobs are in manufactures, industries, in other words industrial jobs. Let us have those, but office jobs are unproductive jobs that eat away the revenues of this country. And today the emphasis is on office jobs and industrial jobs are entirely forgotten. As long as the government fails to take its responsibilities, as long as it leaves the country's administration to a bunch of senior officials against whom it can do nothing because it needs their work and their help, I believe we will continue to pay for the administration, and that is what is happening right now with airports, Mr. Speaker.
Just think that on top of the taxes people were already paying for airports the government is going to charge another 15 per cent to the people who already paid a lot for a ticket, not to improve transportation but to pay for the airport deficit. I do not know if the minister even thought about making a little investigation to find out whether it might be possible to reduce administrative costs before continuing to empty the pockets of Canadians.
With a small population of 22 million or 23 million and budgets running to $57 billion with a deficit of $12 billion, we are spending $69 billion to administer 22 million people, Mr. Speaker. That is not normal. So they simply say that they have to raise general taxes. They are going to make the user pay. But he already does, Mr. Speaker, and he is paying a lot more than he should. Let us take Air Canada, it is understood that deficits are paid by the government, but private airlines serve an entire area. We have already asked the government in the House to assist such small private airlines, but we have to pay.
I live in a region where private airlines operate and if such airlines at least received small subsidies to help them a little. However, the large state airlines are heavily subsidized and we have to pay to make up the deficits incurred by Air Canada. We are people who pay for the chief who travels in a Cadillac while we go on foot. It is the same thing. I think that if the government instead of taking such a step today had tried to help smaller lines, it would not take much to get those lines to improve their service. Air Canada gives excellent service. Small wonder! With all its millions and its deficits we have to pay, and especially with the type of airports like Mirabel we build for it! Now we say we may have made an error! There were no good enough bureaucrats to knew beforehand that
March 23, 1979

Excise Tax Act
such a white elephant would not have enough customers. If they could have built that airport in marble they would have done so. Now we ask passengers to pay for all that, to pay for the government's stupidity.
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-38 gives us an example of maladministration by this government. Once again they want to take money where there is none, namely the users' pockets, but in the same breath they also supply the big monopolies with terrible exemptions. Of that there will be plenty, because big monopolies are protected. Anyway, we will see legislation come forward to show us how monopolies operate, to show us the two major parties competing to save the monopolies. Mr. Speaker, I will conclude by saying simply that we do not agree with all the clauses, especially when it comes to imposing an extra 15 per cent users' tax.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to raise two matters. One involves the changes the government has been making over the years in terms of insulation and energy saving devices, whether they be solar or otherwise. The government has not done anything to encourage the entire energy industry. Whether it be solar, wind or any other type of alternative energy, the government has not done anything at all. I think such help would have been a great advantage in developing the energy industry, and we would have been farther along the road in terms of the development of the forms of energy currently used, such as thermal, nuclear and hydro.
Now the sales tax on solar equipment is being removed. We have known for a long time that we would have to look at solar energy. We are only now part way along the road to removing some of the tax on the energy industry. As I understand it, it will be applied only to a limited number of companies under exceptional circumstances. Thus there will be no easing of manufacturing costs in developing new types of solar energy.
One thing the minister has done indicates the bureaucratic mind of his department better than any other example. I am referring to the matter raised last night by my colleague regarding windows. Suddenly the officials have decided, after a long period of time when we said people should instal bigger windows in their houses, that big windows are a heat loss factor and perhaps a tax should be placed on them. If the officials were only a little smarter, they would realize that if another pane of glass is added the "R" factor would be increased. Instead of using double seal glass, one could use triple seal glass, with three panes, which would result in the same "R" factor as one would from the best insulation.
May I call it one o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

Mr. Speaker, before lunch I had mentioned the fact that the government never seems to be well informed about changes that are taking place in manufacturing. We are continually plagued with the application of taxes for purposes other than that of raising money. With this change we find a tax on windows in the hope that people will curtail the size of windows in their houses as an energy saving measure. I suggest that if we were to adopt the newly designed thermal panes with triple glass we would find they would save more energy in that they are rated with an insulating factor of between R-9 and R-12.
In this field of solar energy and energy saving devices we have been plagued by a lack of knowledge on the part of the department regarding the use of much of this equipment in an experimental way. We are continuing to tax those who want to experiment with various types of energy saving devices such as solar equipment. We write into the bill a provision to reduce the tax on some solar equipment but we keep it on other equipment that may have been used in the past for air conditioning and is therefore more of an energy using device than energy saving. As the industry changes, heat pumps and things of that nature may turn out to be energy saving devices when used in some installations rather than energy wasting.

It is probably safe to say that since the last war we have been receiving letters from the jewellery industry which has been plagued with exceptionally high taxes. There was a luxury tax on jewellery during the war as well as other taxes and in many ways that has continued. The 10 per cent tax added to the 12 per cent tax makes it a very heavily taxed industry. For those manufacturers who make money, there is an additional 40 per cent income tax.
The industry has pointed out to the minister that there is a demand for jewellery in Canada. This government is often accused of being opposed to matrimony; they have been opposed to the marriage structure per se. My colleague would point out very readily that a spouse in this country is an attachment that costs money, not one that provides money. An old age pensioner with a spouse obviously does not receive as much pension and allowances as two people just living together.
The jewellery industry is interested in the matrimonial business but few people are buying jewellery. The industry is subject to a sizeable tax which realizes only a small amount of money. Few young people in this country have not thought of buying jewellery, mostly in connection with a wife to be or a wife already acquired, so much of the industry is involved with matrimony.
About 250 jewellery companies employ 5,600 production workers and 1,500 salaried workers. It is 90 to 95 per cent

Canadian-owned and most of the small, private companies operate in both the wholesale and retail markets. The distribution arm of the industry employs about 11,000 people.
This small industry is subject to an excise tax of 10 per cent on top of the 12 per cent federal sales tax. As well, there is the manufacturing tax and all the other taxes. The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Allmand) has pointed out that between $2 million and $4 million worth of jeweOery is smuggled into this country. That is almost equal to the drug industry. The industry is opposed to smuggling because, first of all, it gives it a bad name and, second, it does not allow it the total business which would be available without smuggled gold and silver.
I am interested in seeing the consumption of gold, whether in gold bullion coins or jewellery, climb to the point that it will ensure the operation of gold mines in Kirkland Lake. For that reason I should like to see smuggling stopped and our own jewellery industry enjoy the increased business. For every job in gold mining, 14 secondary jobs are created.
I do not know whether the minister will do anything about this in the future, indeed, I do not know if he is going to be the minister in the future, but I should like whoever is minister to give consideration to this industry. It is a long time since the last war and the luxury tax on jewellery should be eliminated by now.
When people travel to other countries, they sometimes receive gifts they do not know the value of and get into trouble with the law when they try to bring them home. They are often law abiding people who just do not understand all these taxes.
We would like to finish this bill today, Mr. Speaker, and clear the platter of all those things that have been hanging around for some time.
I would be remiss if I did not join with those people who have been diligent in examining the changes made in this bill which, in effect, rewrite the rules of the House. Quite often our rules are modified in light of changes that take place, with the object of attaining more efficiency and assuring the protection of members. For the past 20 years each parliament has lasted about two and a half years and it is quite possible the changes will be more frequent. Since most members cannot participate in this type of debate, it therefore seems to me it is an abuse for the government to write a change in the rules of the House into legislation. We have seen four or five such bills.
I have some advice that I can give to the next minister of justice. I say to him fire whoever it is in the department that is writing these bills. Otherwise our Standing Orders will be rewritten but there will be no need for them; instead our Standing Orders will be coming from legislation and every time we look at the legislation we will find a different set of Standing Orders under which we must operate.
The rules of parliament, the precedents of Beauchesne, Knowles, May and others who have established them in years gone by have been written after conditions have developed that
Excise Tax Act
have made it advantageous for people to make the changes. These changes are always made with someone saying: "Do not go too far; we still want some rights". Perhaps they should be curtailed but people still want to know what their rights are. Surely even the majority should sympathize with that position. In a democracy no one can say before an election which party will be the government or which party will be the opposition. The rules are written in fairness to both sides.
I would like to see the minister remove everything from clause 16 on. There is absolutely no reason why clause 16 or anything after that should be there. If you want to table the report in parliament, that is fine, but I do not think even that is an absolute necessity. What will we be appealing, Mr. Speaker? We will be appealing the landing tax, the tax on solar energy and tax structures, I suppose even to the extent of whether we like them. If we do not like them, we can change government and the new government will put in different ones.
If it is stated in the bill that 50 members must agree it should be done, it is not a change in the constitution. It is not a major change in the democratic process of the nation. It is not a matter of whether Quebec can secede from the country or of getting rid of the Senate. This is a tax matter. We are saying that 50 members must sign for an appeal. Sometimes it would be impossible to find 50 members in opposition. I can remember when the Liberal party did not have 50 members. Even if they all signed the document, nothing would happen. But they figured they were an important bloc of the day. They considered that they were so important, even with only 50 of them, that they should be the government.
There is absolutely no need for a motion of this kind to be written into a bill. If we want any legislation in parliament to be subject to appeal, we should write a section into the Standing Orders, and we would be able to appeal in an orderly way. That has not been done because members of parliament would not agree. Maybe there are 20, 30, 40 or 50 members here today, and perhaps there were 50 members here yesterday, but it is not likely that 50 members will look at the clause or give any consideration to it. A vote will be taken at the end and the members will be called in, they will not have the faintest notion about this section, but they will pass it.
I suggest that when we write into bills limits for debate, limits for appeals, and limitation on the time in which appeals can be made in allowing parliament to consider any piece of legislation, that is changing the law. That is making a new rule book, Mr. Speaker. We do not have an umpire to make a decision. We do not ask the Speaker of the day to be the umpire. We make the rules and the Standing Orders and establish how they are to be enforced.
Under this piece of legislation and under the last two or three pieces of legislation that we have passed there has been a structure allowing for closure, closure long before a debate is held and closure long before anyone thinks about whether there is any reason closure should apply. It is possible that one day there will be a government with such a small minority there will be a question about closure. On the other hand, it is possible that a government will be elected with so large a

March 23, 1979
Excise Tax Act
majority that they would not consider dignifying closure with making the motion.
There are many things that may happen within the competence of the Standing Orders, the procedures and the precedents that have been established by the British parliament over the last five hundred years and by the Canadian parliament in its one hundredth year. All these precedents have a purpose. They were designed to maintain democracy, allowing a government to govern and the opposition to make their position known and to be prepared to form the government if that is necessary.	'
I firmly believe that this minister is democratic. Some of the ministers who have introduced legislation are not-for instance, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) and several other ministers. But I am sure this minister is willing to use the democratic process. He is well aware that there are disadvantages to a democracy. It means you have to hear the other fellow and also that you must listen to him for longer than you want to. But he is also well aware that maybe he will be the other fellow next year or in the future. Therefore he does not want to hamstring the system so that it is inflexible.
It is a disgrace that civil servants who think that they have reached the stage of being untouchable can write this kind of closure legislation and that we are stupid enough to pass it. No member of parliament should support this bill with this kind of a clause in it. In my opinion it would be in the interests of the minister to withdraw clause 16 of the bill when we reach it.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my remarks in connection with this particular legislation will be very brief. However, I wish to make a few remarks in the presence of the minister after hearing the excellent speech of my colleague, the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters).
I wish to lend support to the proposition put forward by members of the opposition generally with respect to the growing tendency on the part of this government to introduce in various pieces of legislation provisions by which parliament is being downgraded, the rights of individual parliamentarians are being diminished, and there is the process we find creeping into more and more legislation whereby, with respect to legislation before the House, the rights of parliamentarians are determined in advance by way of closure.
I want to remind the minister that we have had this provision brought to our attention in legislation before the House now on three consecutive bills. It is not because of a unique or unusual provision in the bill that is required by the nature of this legislation. A similar provision was included in the referendum bill, a bill dealing with the constitution of this country. The rights of parliamentarians are being stomped upon by this government, ostensibly because it is a matter that will be dealt with only in times of emergency. The bill in fact covers a very wide ambit of constitutional change. The rights of parliamentarians are being curtailed. We are limited in the amount of debate we can have. That goes to the very root of our constitution, the very basis of our country.

The next piece of legislation the government came forward with was the bill dealing with petroleum allocation, the so-called energy bill. What do we find in that legislation? In the event the government determines that we have a perceived or apprehended energy shortage, not a shortage de facto, there is a provision in that bill to limit debate in this House on such emergency to three days.
The next piece of legislation the government brought forward dealt with the Excise Tax Act. As members on this side quite rightly point out, the tendency of this government is to downplay parliament, to diminish the rights of each and every member, including those on the government side. Here we have a similar kind of provision. It has the effect of limiting debate with regard to particular orders filed under clause 15.
I hope and trust the minister will address himself to this provision during the course of committee of the whole. There is a growing concern not only in this House but by editorial writers and indeed the people of Canada that this government has come to the conclusion that the rights of parliament should be curtailed on each and every occasion where it may be inconvenient for the government to explain or to bring a matter before parliament.
There is a debate.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader

On clause 1-
Excise Tax Act

Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the minister could elaborate on this clause. Perhaps he can give us some background as to who is responsible for initiating this clause.
Perhaps at the same time he could attempt to justify his position. How can he agree that the air transportation tax should be almost doubled, particularly during a difficult period of restraint? He is asking Canadians generally to exercise restraint. He is asking labour and industry to exercise restraint. Yet here is a service being provided by the federal government in respect to which the fee is virtually being doubled. The increase certainly far exceeds the rate of inflation in this country, notwithstanding the fact that the rate of inflation is very high.
I am sure the minister heard my remarks yesterday when I read into the record some of the innumerable deficiencies which the Auditor General had noted in his last report in connection with mismanagement, failure to control and cost over-runs for which the Minister of Transport is responsible. The increase in tax represents an attempt to recover those losses, to pay for the waste, the extravagance and the mismanagement which has gone on.
I would also draw attention to the adverse impact this measure would probably have on our tourism account. Yesterday I quoted the government's own report, the recommendations of which run directly counter to government policy. I pointed out that air transportation is a necessity in many of the remote areas in this country, not a luxury. In many cases it is the only mode of travel available and the doubling of the tax will have its greatest impact upon those who rely solely on air transport.
I am sure the minister has been caught in a squeeze. I do not think this is his idea. If it is, I should like him to say so. I think he has been painted into a corner by the Minister of Transport, who has lost control of his department and cannot exercise the kind of management which it needs so badly. It is all very well to talk about user-pay, but the minister tells us that the true principle of user-pay is not being applied. I should like him to elaborate. Is it the intention to attempt to ensure full cost recovery in all cases where government services are provided? The situation now is that the cost of providing man-made facilities and other services relating to the travelling public is the highest in the western world. It is certainly higher here than it is in the United States.
There is at present a dispute going on between Canada and the United States about air fares. Surely in a period of deregulation, Canadians and people generally in North America associate deregulation with cheaper fares. In this case American airlines have been prevented from bringing in cheaper air travel between our two countries. This whole scenario is wrapped up with the cost recovery scheme of the Minister of Transport.
I should like the Minister of Finance to tell us who was the originator of this proposal. Was it he, or was it the Minister of Transport? I believe the hon. gentleman is carrying the can for

March 23, 1979
Excise Tax Act
the Minister of Transport. Does he agree with the statement of the deputy minister of transport who roundly criticized the Auditor General for calling attention to cases of inadequate cost control and poor financial management within the department?
The deputy minister of finance criticized the Auditor General and suggested that he should mind his own business. Yet the Auditor General is the custodian of the public purse; he is the financial caretaker, the watchdog on behalf of Canadians generally. We in this House have lost control over the public purse by reason of the present committee structure and the closure rule. The Auditor General is now the only one equipped to carry out this task, and he has pointed out that the Minister of Transport has mismanaged the affairs of the department-that there has been waste, mismanagement and failure to consult effectively with the users of the services provided.
I should like the Minister of Finance to make his position clear because we are placing ourselves in a strange situation: on one hand we are attempting to redress the imbalance of our tourist account, while on the other we are imposing heavy penalties on the air travelling public.

Mr. Chairman, the airports are running up operational deficits which the Minister of Transport wants to reduce by increasing the tax which is specifically allocated for the administration of those airports. I am in a difficult position because the hon. member is arguing about the management of the Department of Transport, its philosophy in terms of air operations and so on. I am not the Minister of Transport; I am the Minister of Finance. The hon. member asked me a question and I answer, yes, the Minister of Transport wanted me to increase the tax in order to cope with the problem of the deficit in airport operations.
I will concede that what is proposed represents a high increase. But there will still remain a huge deficit of $123 million in the operation of the airports so the amount which would be raised would certainly not be sufficient to operate the expensive and elaborate system we have established. Of course, when you travel in Canada you have the advantage of the best airports anywhere. We have fine airports in Vancouver, in Winnipeg, in Montreal, at Mirabel, in Halifax and so on. We have a very good system but it is extremely expensive, and in order to pay for part of this operation the Minister of Transport has asked me to increase the tax. The hon. member asked me who was the promoter. It was the Minister of Transport.

Has the minister satisfied himself that cuts could not have been made within the operations of the ministry which would have produced the same amount of money, $72 million, as this tax is expected to generate in the first year of its operation? Further, the Minister of Transport has served notice that landing fees and fees for associated service related to the movement of aircraft are going to increase by six times over the next eight years, at a rate of approximately 30 per cent a year. Is the minister not concerned about the impact this will have on the travelling public

and the impact it could conceivably have of further aggravating our tourist trade deficit?

Mr. Chairman, I think at all times the government has to be preoccupied with increases in the cost of many services. I am not aware of any admission by the Minister of Transport that those costs will increase six times in the next ten years.
They will.

If that is the situation, I have the impression that that is too much, and I think we have to make sure that we live within our means. That is one topic I have been talking about since I was president of the treasury board. We have to reduce the level of increase in the expenditures of the federal government. The hon. member cannot deny that the year before I was president of the treasury board the increase in the level of expenditures of government from year to year, 197475, was 25 per cent and that during my tenure I reduced it to around 10 per cent. That was less than the gross national product. However, this is a constant battle we have to keep fighting, and I am pleased that the hon. member subscribes to the principle that we have to control our expenditures.

Mr. Chairman, the minister obviously is not advised. The officials who are with him at the table apparently are not in a position to advise him. The fact is that with these increased revenues there will be upwards of $90 million in surplus operational revenue for the operation of our 23 major airports. What may or may not be intended is to use the enormous operational surplus to pay off debts for white elephants like Mirabel and Pickering and to make up for the mismanagement and bungling at Calgary. That may very well be. Indeed, it seems quite obvious that that is what is happening. Because of the movement of these funds into a single revolving fund, the minister's colleague, the Minister of Transport, is effectively removing from us in this chamber any real ability to scrutinize the fund and what is being done with it.
Leaving that to one side, the surplus in operational revenue will approach $90 million within the next three to four years. The question of my colleague, the hon. member for Vegreville, is whether the minister is satisfied with this type of rip-off of the Canadian traveller, not to mention our capacity to continue to attract tourists to our country to try to offset our account deficit on that side of the ledger. Does the minister not think that this is in fact a rip-off, and is he not prepared to direct himself to the question of whether the generation of operational surpluses of this magnitude is unjustified and uncalled for?

Mr. Chairman, I have explained that the total operation of airports is in a deficit position. The hon. member referred to major airports, but we have to provide some services in isolated areas. Even with this tax increase there will still be a deficit of $123 million.

That is a deficit on capital and everything else, not the operational surplus.
March 23, 1979

It is for the total operation. The Minister of Transport appears in other fora. He appears in committes of the House and defends the policies of the Department of Transport. This measure is a move by us to increase a tax. I am not the minister who should be called upon to respond regarding the administration of airports. I have to take full responsibility for this tax increase, but I am not in a position to debate airport operations. I am not the Minister of Transport, nor do I want to be.

Mr. Chairman, I am not asking the Minister of Finance to assume responsibility for transport in this country, although God knows he probaby would do a better job than the job being done by his colleague. That is not my point. Surely the Minister of Finance has some responsibility to scrutinize the formal requests which come to him from his colleague to increase their departmental capacity to garner revenues. That is what we are talking about. We are not talking about running airports at all. We are talking about whether the generation of a potential surplus from operational revenues at the expense of the travelling Canadian public and tourists is in keeping with practices which are acceptable to the Minister of Finance.
Will we have full user-pay? Will the Minister of Finance direct himself to that simple question? Is he prepared to direct the Minister of Transport to direct VIA Rail to operate cost effectively? Is that what the minister is talking about? Is that what he is trying to tell Canadians? Let him justify with one single reason, if he can, the right of the Minister of Transport on the backs of Canadian air travellers to have an operational surplus upwards of $90 million. As the minister knows, we do not pay the capital cost of operational profits. We never have. This will be an artificial profit to offset, behind the back of parliament, the whims and fancies of an already well demonstrated inadequate Minister of Transport.
There are 101 reasons why the Minister of Transport should resign and go to the Senate along with the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. There are 101 reasons, and I am citing one $90 million reason. Please! Surely we are entitled to some explanation.
Mr. .Chretien: Mr. Chairman, the hon. member has heard that we have a surplus, but we do not have a surplus. After this increase in taxes there will still be a deficit of $123 million in the operation of the airports of Canada. If I accepted the theory of full recovery, the tax increase would have to be threefold. We had to balance that. We decided to reduce the deficit. This tax increase will reduce the tax deficit by $72 million. There will still be $123 million which will have to be paid by the treasury directly from the consolidated revenues of Canada. The hon. member assumes that there will be a slush fund that the Minister of Finance can use, but that is not the case. This will make up just part of the deficit. Canada has a small population, and distances are long. Transportation is quite expensive, and there is no miracle. The money we spend is the money we collect. If we do not collect it one way we have to collect it another way, unless we cut services.
