The opposition transport critic argues that the Department of Transport has too many officers and provides too much service and that the minister could have cut even deeper than he did. He can argue that.
No. The Auditor General says that, not me.

Nobody has denied the fact that there is a deficit in the operation of our airports. We are not meeting that deficit. We do not want to hurt travellers too much. We do not want to hurt tourists who come here. This is a question of judgment. It is one of the pleasures and responsibilities of the Minister of Finance not to be in agreement at all times with all people. This afternoon I have to increase one tax, but this is the first time in a year and a half that I have increased taxes. I have reduced taxes since I have been Minister of Finance. In the last budget I reduced personal income tax to the tune of $1.5 billion. I reduced sales taxes to the tune of $1.2 billion. It is true that I am now raising $72 million, but I cannot be accused of being a minister who has increased many taxes. The hon. member would like to blame the Minister of Transport for this increase, but by the nature of my job I am responsible for tax increases and I take full responsibility. I never try to wash my hands.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Chairman, as I understand the increase in the transportation tax for air passengers, the revenues produced will go into a revolving fund to be used for the airport deficit and perhaps to build airports. Clause 1 would allow the conversion of this tax to a user charge, and therefore the House of Commons would not have the authority we have today to discuss such a charge in the committee or in this chamber. The minister will then have the power-as it says here that the cost will go up six times and the Minister of Finance himself said that this is too much, with which I agree-to use this charge to increase the moneys he will get to offset the deficit. My concern here is that as I look at airports across the country, I see overbuilding at a number of airports and underbuilding at some others. I can quote examples of overbuilding, such as at Mirabel which cost $700 million and now has a deficit of $50 million a year, and at Calgary airport which cost $138 million and will probably have large deficits for a number of years. Then we can look at airports like the airport at Fort McMurray, and the Edmonton airport, both of which have the same number of landings as Calgary or Mirabel but are not large enough for the number of people going through them. The people there are hoarded through the airports.
Which airport in Edmonton are you referring to?

The international airport, the only one under federal control. People there are hoarded through in long lines in the basement. The area for people arriving from

Excise Tax Act
abroad was built in the times of the old Vanguards with 70 passengers. Now sometimes two 747s land at the same time and people getting off these planes have to line up in rows almost city blocks long, waiting for their turn to get to the customs area. This is not fair to these people.
We are now asking parliament to give the minister authority to change this tax to a user-charge, and therefore parliament will no longer have the authority to question it. I am concerned about this change to the user-charge. What is the reason for it, and what guarantees will parliament have that there will not be overbuilding in some areas and underbuilding in other areas, such as I have outlined?

Mr. Chairman, I have nothing to add to the comments of the hon. member. We are discussing of course clauses 14 and 15 dealing with the system as introduced in that legislation to allow the automatic transfer following a debate in the House, because the whole matter could have been done under an order in council, but the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) suggested that the House should have an opportunity to discuss it under a negative resolution. The whole matter could have been dealt with through an order in council, but the Minister of Transport, being a fine democrat, wanted to give hon. members an opportunity to hold a debate. Apparently, they would rather have left the whole matter in the hands of the Minister of Transport. If the House unanimously agrees that it be done through an order in council, we could discuss the matter at length when we reach clauses 14 and 15.1 was very pleased to see-

-that we were ready to let parliament discuss that for five hours. Apparently now they would prefer not to debate it at all. We are very pleased and consider ourselves fortunate to be debating it on a negative resolution which was not in existence before. I am surprised that both the Conservatives and members of the NDP are so traditionalist in these matters. It is annoying, or perhaps surprising, that I always find myself defending the British system.
In the British House of Commons there are all sorts of regulations permitting bills to be passed in one or two days, allowing time allocation and closure with no problem, but when I want to implement the British tradition, being the good French peasouper that I am, I find those Anglophones opposite opposing me. It is unbelievable. I do not know what is wrong here. I am proud of being the product of bicultural Canada. But let us wait and see what happens when we are on clause 14.
Triculture.

Or tricultural Canada, if you prefer. I will be able to debate that provision when we come to that clause.
When the hon. member talks about big airports and overbuilding, I am reminded of the time when I was a backbench member of parliament and was travelling to Edmonton in 1967

because, as the hon. member knows, the hon. member for Vegreville is almost my member of parliament because my family on my mother's side is from there. So we were going to Edmonton in 1967.
And they vote Conservative.

I think they vote Liberal, but sometimes they find themselves lonesome, just like the Tories in my riding, who feel terrible. So in 1967 I visited the Edmonton airport for the first time and I noticed that nobody used that airport which was some way away from the city; everyone wanted to use the downtown airport. Everyone referred to the international airport at Edmonton as a white elephant. Now we find that it is used a lot. The same thing will happen probably at Mirabel.
When I visited the international airport at Edmonton in 1967, the airport had been empty for the previous ten years and it was the topic of conversation. The bureaucrat who had recommended its creation had some wisdom, but no one at that time realized it. It is probably the same thing with Mirabel. It is probably one of the most efficient airports. In fact it is so efficient that it looks empty because passengers just go through it and are out within minutes.
There is nobody there.

The Russians came to see it. They would like to have the same thing.
With regard to this negative resolution, my friend, who has a funny name for his riding anyway-
Wetaskiwin.
We will debate the resolution when we reach clause 15, and I hope we will reach it soon.
Mr. Chairman, the minister, in his usual effervescent manner, has attempted, quite successfully, to diffuse some of the very important issues we are trying to raise.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: He gave me the hiccups.
He spoke about his maternal foundations in the constituency of Vegreville.
I am from Vegreville too.

And now we hear the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway has the great distinction of coming from Vegreville also. The only problem is that she was led astray and became involved with the Liberal pack. That is really unfortunate.
The minister, as my colleague from Wetaskiwin pointed out, has referred to the proposal to increase landing fees and other related services six times-that is a fact and the minister can take my word for it because this is common knowledge in air transportation circles and in the Ministry of Transport.
I am surprised when he says that we have the services. They have to be paid for and, if we do not get them here, we get
March 23, 1979

them elsewhere. I am surprised at him taking such a stand. He is an enterprising person and he knows that competition is keen. He is a competitive person, and the fact of the matter is that if charges of this magnitude are going to be imposed, we will clearly be in a very unfavourable position relative to our counterparts.
For example, the basis of the information I have is provided by the Air Transport Association of Canada which, incidentally, represents some 90 per cent or 95 per cent of all airline revenue in Canada. They point out that the landing fees of a DC9-that is landing fees only, not en route service charges, navigational charges, and an assortment of other charges-are approximately $45. At many U.S. points that charge is only $20 to $25. At the end of the eight year program, that charge will be over $200 in Canada, or more than that per passenger in landing fees alone. A Boeing 747 landing at Vancouver from Toronto would be paying about $1,800, or $4.50 per passenger. The same aircraft landing at Kansas City with about the same passenger volume would pay $200, $400 in Chicago, and $800 in Seattle, which is one of the highest charges in the U.S.
When we take that into consideration relative to the impact on our tourist industry, can the minister tell us whether he agrees with the statement in the report of the sector task force on the Canadian tourism industry? It is indicated in that report that the airport user-pay policy makes Canadian air transportation non-competitive with that of the United States and is detrimental to Canadian tourism. The Minister of Finance is in charge of the over-all economy. He is interested in bolstering the dollar. He is interested in revitalizing the economy. Does he agree with that statement?

Mr. Chairman, we are dealing with a tax increase, yet we are debating transport policies which are the responsibility of my colleague, the Minister of Transport. Of course I want the tourism deficit to diminish. At the same time we must pay for the services we are providing, which is always the dilemma we face. The hon. member should know that if we do not have any landing fee or any taxes, we will have to collect it in another way. If we do not collect it one way, we will collect it another way. Of course I do not want to increase the $10.7 billion cash requirement this year. I am glad to see the hon. member has the same preoccupation as I on that. I hope he will talk with his leader who has been promising, if his party should form the next government, to cut back taxes to the tune of $6 billion on top of the $10.7 billion deficit which exists at this time.
Also we are talking about cutting out waste.

When we provided various cuts, every member opposite double talked about those issues. They rose and asked why we did not give a subsidy for this or why we cut the subsidy for that. Also they asked why we were not increasing a certain subsidy. Of course it is easy when one is a member of the opposition. But because of that double-talking,

hon. members opposite will not have a chance at trying their hand at running the government. Some months ago I thought opposition members had some chance, but they have fumbled it. They became crazy and talked about stimulative deficits. Even the financial critic indicated that it was to be an instant deficit, but I call it a phantom deficit. He indicated that it would be there for a month only. We keep our books for 12 months, so there cannot be a deficit for one month. That is why Conservative members lost their chance at finding the facts. If hon. members have some good facts, they should go before the committee and explain them to the minister.
We have some good facts.

They should give the minister some help. I require the help of hon. members opposite in those fields. In fact, I require the help of everyone. I want to make sure that government expenditure will not increase. I appreciate the good work of the hon. member. He is trying to keep the operation of airports as healthy as possible. But we cannot deny that there is a deficit of $193.7 million in the operation of airports. With the imposition of this tax it will be reduced by $72 million, and I will be left with a deficit of $121 million. If hon. members would like to give me some tips about from where I can get this $121 million, other than cutting programs in the Department of Transport, I would be interested in hearing them. There is nothing I would like to add to the list of people and programs which should be cut in the Department of Transport.

When the minister speaks of stimulative deficits and what not, I should like to remind him that he is four-fifths wrong and one-fifth right. If he is looking for suggestions of areas in which the fat might be cut, or where better operational efficiencies and financial management control can be injected, I invite him to read the report of the Auditor General. The minister is a good friend of the Auditor General. He knows the importance of the Auditor General. He does not have to take any advice from me and we do not have to go to committee.
Just to dwell on that point for a moment, the minister knows well that when we were considering the estimates on transport, we had the minister before the committee for a couple of hours, or three hours at the most. The structure of the committee system does not give us the opportunity to deal with these specific issues and to challenge some of the spending programs of the government. Thank God for the Auditor General! The minister should review the facts clearly. If he did so, he would not be as eager to accept the recommendations of the Department of Transport. If the minister looked at the facts very carefully and analytically, I am sure he would tell the Minister of Transport to clean up his act. That is what we are suggesting the Minister of Finance should do.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader

Mr. Chairman, it was not my intention to participate at this point, but now that the minister has made an unnecessary and rather shoddy political intervention, I felt

March 23, 1979
Excise Tax Act
it was only right to rise and bring the minister back to the provision with which we are dealing.
If the Minister of Finance does not want to answer the question, that is one thing, but I am sure he is anxious to get the bill through. The Minister of Finance should let the committee and the country know whether he agrees with that method of dealing with this overwhelming deficit brought about-and I am not being partisan here-in large part by the bungling and incompetence of the Department of Transport under a succession of Liberal ministers. Can the minister give an assessment as to whether this particular tax is counterproductive in terms of international tourism? Does he think that we have gone far enough in this connection and that we must look in terms of the over-all operation? Perhaps this is one instance in terms of taxation policy in which we will do ourselves more harm by increasing this particular tax rather than having it borne by general taxation.
Does the minister think there is something to be said as to how he justifies the imposition of this tax? The minister admitted that it will have a detrimental effect on tourism and travel in Canada. That is what we want to hear about. We do not want to hear partisan political flim-flam. We want to deal with the bill. We want to get down to the nub of the problem before us. The Minister of Finance should be concerned with fiscal policy. Does he have any ideas respecting what level of taxation will cause a serious problem to Canadian tourism? Is this particular tax getting to the point where it will discourage people from utilizing air services and travelling by air in Canada?

Mr. Chairman, this is of course a matter of judgment. Taxes must be paid in every airport. I am told, for instance, that the tax in the United States is 8 per cent with no ceiling provided and that it can reach a higher amount than in Canada. Moreover, had I not been concerned about the level of taxation for tourism, I might have urged the Minister of Transport to recover the full $193 million, but I did not do so. Of course, this is a matter of judgment.
We decided not to exceed $72 million, and this may be somewhat too high. I would have preferred not to have any increase. I would certainly not have wished for an increase, because I recognize that this can be an additional cost for those who visit Canada. However, I believe that in general, most air travellers in Canada are not tourists. They are for the most part foreigners and businessmen who travel by plane in Canada to conduct their daily business and not necessarily as tourists. This is why we did not exceed $72 million, because I believe that if I had insisted that we should recover the full $193 million, this would have had a very negative effect.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader

I think the answer of the minister underlines one of the problems we have in terms of fiscal and taxation policies. It is obvious the minister has had no input into this particular tax and has not given one bit of consider-

ation to the over-all taxation levels. He is simply the errand boy with respect to this particular taxation. He has not been consulted and is here as the spokesman for the Minister of Transport, saying that in fact this particular provision has nothing whatever to do with whether we are going to have a deficit. He simply carries out the orders of the Minister of Transport and that minister has his own little theory about the user having to pay.
And he smiles.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Yes, physiognomy was the term used in respect of the Minister of Transport who has the ability to smile. I simply say this, without smiling at all, that it is an interesting admission the minister has now made that, as far as he is concerned, he has little control over the level of taxation or this element of taxation by the government, and he is simply here as an errand boy to carry out the philosophy of user-pay which has been imposed as a burden on him by the Minister of Transport. It is interesting to note that the minister feels this has nothing to do with taxation, but results from the Minister of Transport's theory which will be inflicted upon all the people of Canada who use the transportation facilities of this country. Those are the people who will bear the burden of this philosophy. It should be remembered, no matter what kind of rhetoric the minister may indulge in during the course of the election campaign, that this is the policy of this government. I think I have made my point.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall clause 1 carry?
Carried.

On division.
Clause 1 agreed to.
Clauses 2 and 3 agreed to.
On clause 4-Consumption or sales tax of nine per cent.

Mr. Chairman, I think we have reached page 4 of the bill and that clause which states:
There shall be imposed, levied and collected a consumption or sales tax of nine per cent on the sale price of all goods-
This represents a reduction in the sales tax from 12 per cent to 9 per cent, which we on this side of the House welcome. However, we on this side of the House have frequently raised points regarding the application of this tax in respect of stock in the hands of a dealer as inventory, on which the dealer has been forced to pay the tax at the higher level and must therefore absorb the 3 per cent differential. This has amounted in many cases to a great deal of money and has imposed severe hardships on the dealer, particularly small dealers caught in the position of having rather large inventories.
It is interesting to note that in the ways and means motion tabled in the House on the evening of the presentation of the budget it was made clear that the new rate will apply to sales by manufacturers and licensed wholesalers on goods sold or
March 23, 1979

delivered to purchasers and on goods imported into Canada or taken out of warehouse for consumption after November 16, 1978, and that the reduction in the general rate does not have a termination date. That statement generally will be interpreted as meaning when the product is sold to the retail customer, and that is the point with which we take issue.
There are precedents to show that when sales or excise taxes have previously been reduced or removed, funds have been reimbursed to dealers with inventories or stock on hand at the time. I believe there was a precedent in 1958, another in 1974, and it seems to me there was another in 1961 when an excise tax was removed. Inventories in the hands of dealers at the time were subject to remission by the Government of Canada.
We believe the application of this particular measure is very harsh on some dealers, particularly dealers in automobiles, large industrial equipment dealers, dealers handling refrigerators and a host of other items. I do not think the Minister of Finance, being a great supporter of small business and small enterprise, and a believer in the private enterprise system and in the importance of small enterprise to this country, would think otherwise than that a remission should be due and forthcoming to those people who have been left with inventories on hand at the time of the introduction of the budget.
With that in mind, Mr. Chairman, I should like to introduce an amendment as follows:
That clause 4 of Bill C-38 be amended by striking out line 39 on page 4, substituting therefor the following:
"Goods which had not by November 16, 1978, been delivered to the final
retail purchaser."
I have this amendment in both official languages and I will make copies available to members on the government side.

Mr. Chairman, I have written many letters in this regard. I have a great deal of sympathy for the suggestion by the hon. member. We have reduced the tax on almost all items taxable in many fields and it would have been almost impossible for the government to reimburse everyone affected. I have recognized the situation in the letters I have written to automobile dealers, and they are the ones who have raised the most flak. I have been in touch with them and have received some communications. We felt that if we did this for the automobile dealers we would have to do it for everybody else. When we did this previously it was in respect of one exceptional case when there was a reduction on one item, namely, trucks. That was easy because it was easily definable and there was no other sector involved. Sometimes we must have rough justice when a variety of items are involved. We have to keep everybody under the same umbrella in the same circumstances. In these circumstances every aspect of the tax is reduced from 12 per cent to 9 per cent and, unfortunately, it is not possible to make a distinction.
I appreciate the efforts of the hon. member, but I cannot accept this proposition which would in effect increase the deficit of the government by some $351 million. I am sure the hon. member will be shocked to find that he might be personally responsible for increasing the deficit to the tune of $351
Excise Tax Act
million. I had to give him that explanation and I am sure he did not think it would involve so much money. Under the present circumstances I cannot accept the amendment, a move which would cost the treasury more than $351 million.

Mr. Chairman, in attempting to justify or explain his position, surely the minister is not telling us that he expects the poor dealers to pay the 3 per cent tax differential. Surely he is not suggesting that they should pay that 3 per cent, but that is exactly what is happening. Having regard to automobile dealers, when the tax was reduced the retail price was reduced automatically, and the dealer who was stuck with the product on his lot had to reduce his price accordingly. Surely he is not suggesting they should pay the $350 million.

Mr. Chairman, by this time I think most of the dealers will have sold their inventory, otherwise they would be in bad shape. There is always a problem from one day to the other when the tax system is changed. In previous budgets that raised taxes, those people who already had inventory paid less tax than those who bought later, but they never suggested that they would make too much money and should return the money to the government. When taxes were increased the person who had goods before the budget made a profit through having paid less taxes on them.
It is too late now. The budget was presented on November 16 and the inventory has probably been depleted by this time. We cannot make a distinction between car dealers and other dealers. If we were to accept this proposition it would cost the treasury $350 million. It would be irresponsible to add that much to the deficit of the government.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have a few things to say about this provision. The minister knew when the motion was put in the budget that this was going to cost the treasury $350 million. New automobile models had just been introduced, so surely the officials knew inventories were at a high level in anticipation of Christmas sales. I say this was a cynical move. The ministry knew this $350 million would be swallowed by the retailers. Some of the large ones can write it off through taxes, but the small and medium-sized retailers had to swallow a good portion of it, and so it is a direct loss to them. I say the minister and his officials were totally irresponsible and they should be censured for acting in such a cynical way. I see some of the officials at the table smiling; they would smile on the other side of their faces if they were in the business.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to add a few words. I suggest the government was most incompetent and irresponsible. If it was the intention not to allow dealers to take advantage of the reduction in tax on the stock on hand, then it was a cynical move and a burden on hundreds and thousands of dealers across Canada.
There is some ambiguity in the provision covering this proposal in the ways and means motion. The part dealing with the general sales tax reduction states that the new rates will apply to sales by manufacturers and all licensed wholesalers on

March 23, 1979

goods that are sold or delivered to the purchaser as well as goods imported into Canada or taken out of a warehouse for consumption after November 16, 1978. To the uneducated eye that provision means that the dealer could have the benefit of the reduction on stock on hand. That is in the publication put out by the minister as an explanation of the ways and means motion. When clarification was sought by the thousands of dealers upon whom a great financial burden is imposed they were told that a bill would be introduced which would specify that the provision does not apply to the stock on hand at the time of the budget.
I want to support the proposition put forward by the hon. member for Vegreville. It reflects what appears to have been the minister's intention at the time of the budget. Perhaps the problem arose as a result of an oversight on the minister's part, but if he had the honesty and the courage to stand up and admit that he was wrong, we could at least dismiss it as another instance of incompetence. I would like to know what the minister feels about the burden he has placed upon the hundreds and thousands of dealers, small businessmen and taxpayers in this country, who have been severely punished through this incompetent provision. I strongly support the amendment put forward by the hon. member for Vegreville.

Second, I am not an expert on how car dealers operate, but I know there was a shift in price because of the models and many of the inventory-
You are absolutely wrong.

Now the opposition seems to argue that I should not have cut taxes. When the tax is changed from day one to day two, the situation is just the same as if the

electricity costs for the garage went up. In that case they do not go to the municipality and ask to be reimbursed. When there are other cost increases from day one to day two, that is part of the system. I think some of the costs can be absorbed. The Chair can look into the procedural point, and perhaps the best way to dispose of it is to face the reality that we cannot afford to lose $350 million. We knew that, and I faced the flak. speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order, please. Perhaps before continuing we should formally propose the amendment. In answer to the concern an hon. member had as to the acceptability of the amendment, in my opinion procedurally it is quite acceptable. There are many provisions for that in Beauchesne's fifth edition at citations Nos. 526 and 527 where it says that reductions can be made in committee so long as the existing tax is not increased. Therefore, the amendment is acceptable. The question is on the amendment, moved by Mr. Mazankowski:
That Bill C-38 be amended by striking out line 39 on page four, and substituting therefor the following:
"Goods which had not by November 16, 1978, been delivered to the final
retail purchaser."

Mr. Chairman, I hope the minister realizes that sometimes repentance is good for the soul. There is still time for him to repent because of the error, and perhaps gross misjudgment, he has made. I make this statement with regard to the timing of the proposed taxation. Perhaps the tax should have been changed to coincide with the change in models, namely, from one model year to another. This does not necessarily apply only to the automobile industry, it applies through the whole system including such things as fridges, stoves, etc.
New models usually come on the market in the months of August, September and October. If the government, and the minister, had chosen that period of time to make the change, there would not have been that high inventory on tap with which these small dealers were caught.
I want to explain to the minister something of which he may not be aware. Canada relies to a great deal for its financial stability on the small towns across the nation. I am speaking of small towns with populations of 6,000, 5,000, 4,000 and less. It was the dealers in these small towns who were caught in the middle by the change in taxation at that time of the year. In many cases they have nothing to say as to the number of cars or other products they have on tap at that time. Companies send out products as soon as they are available. It is possible that orders had been placed a year previously. These dealers
March 23, 1979

were then caught with a high inventory of new models. If the minister can see his way clear to make some adjustment to these people, it will be of real benefit to the small business people who form the backbone of the Canadian economy.
I realize that dealers in large centres can absorb this loss much better than in smaller centres. It is the smaller dealers in small centres who are caught. I hope the minister will repent and give some consideration to this request. I would ask him to be fair to these people who are hurt so badly by the timing of his legislation.

Mr. Chairman, I enter this debate because I come from a small riding with 40 small communities, all of which have two or three small dealerships in each community. I have received letters from each one. I suppose it would take me 15 minutes to put them all on the record. I will not do that but I want to be sure the minister understands that there are communities in this country which have dealerships in them run by people who are not rich. These people operate small businesses. Total income for the year for these people is possibly $15,000 to $20,000 on which their families must live. Because of this decrease in tax at a time when their inventories were large, many of those dealers have told me privately that they have lost between $6,000 to $10,000 this year.
I have a letter from an international truck dealer in which it is mentioned that because of the lowering in tax there is a difference of about $1,800 on one unit. If he has 10 units on his lot, although at the time I think he had six or seven units, you can understand the kind of loss he would face in his income.
This amendment asks that consideration be given to those dealers who had units on the lot in stock before November 16, 1978. One of the dealers said:
The problem relates to the removal of federal sales tax on trucks of 16000 G.V.W. and larger as announced in last week's budget.
It is my understanding that the tax removal only applies to those units manufactured after the budget date. You will realize that dealers having large inventories will stand to lose considerable by having to absorb the amount of tax. It is my considered opinion that all units unsold and dealers inventory should be exempted.
This is exactly what this amendment does.
I have another letter from a small dealership in the city of Wetaskiwin. He says:
I would like to go on record that in no way can the dealer be expected to absorb the costs of this tax. You can be sure the customer will be insisting on a rebate and rightly so, but not at the expense of the dealer.
Consumers who visit a dealer following the tax decrease mention car prices should drop between $300 to $500. They would look at various cars and ask the dealer if he had knocked down the price. In order to keep his customers the dealer had to answer, "Yes, because of the budget last night the price of vehicles has dropped". But he had to refer to the 10 or 20 vehicles he had on his lot and say; "I am sorry, you will have to buy one of these cars in stock at the old price until I get rid of this stock." In view of that, the prospective purchaser would go to Edmonton or perhaps another larger centre where a dealer sells thousands of cars per year. These
Excise Tax Act
larger dealers can put any loss sustained over a much greater volume. The loss does not harm them in the same way it does a smaller dealer.
The minister should show some compassion to the small dealers and accept the amendment put forward by the hon. member for Vegreville.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the minister in the course of his reply clearly misunderstood what I had been talking about. I said hundreds and thousands. The minister is trying to argue what is a very weak case for him on this particular provision. I am satisfied the minister came into the budge with a statement, realized his error afterwards, and has had to backtrack and make explanations ever since when he realized the full implication of the provision. I wish the minister would get up and admit that that was the case.
The minister tried to suggest that we are only dealing with car dealers. I have to concede that car dealers are an example of independent Canadian businessmen who are most seriously affected by this particular revision. These businessmen have inventories of equipment and goods to be sold to the public, worth quite a substantial amount of money. Naturally people in that particular industry are the ones who will feel the pinch of this rather inept dealing on the part of the federal government with respect to reduction of tax. We are not just talking about car dealers. I hope everyone understands that. We are dealing with retailers of every description who carry goods to which the manufacturers sales tax applies.
Budget night was a great night for the minister with the red rose in his lapel, the new shoes, and his hair combed. It was a great television production. I recall it vividly. He was surrounded by his sycophants who applauded every time the minister raised his hand to give the signal. A lot of people made the mistake of believing the minister when he said there would be a 3 per cent reduction.
I have learned never to argue with the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway, not because she is right but because it is just too much trouble. She is a good friend of mine. I will not say more because I know she does not want to interrupt the thrust of my argument.
When the minister makes a presentation in terms of budgetary matters, it is extremely serious when he conveys an impression to Canadians, including consumers and dealers, that a particular tax provision will become effective on the date of the budget. If the minister understood this all along, he should have clarified it in the course of his remarks, indicating that it would not take effect until some time down the road. The implication in the budget papers and the general statement left a distinct and clear impression.
I pointed out the provision in the budget papers, that this would apply effective that date on all sales which took place after the budget was brought down. The parliamentary secretary agrees with me. I appreciate that because the minister would not do it.

That was in the budget speech of the minister on November 16. It was made abundantly clear there would not be rebates for inventories on hand.
That's flim-flam.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is standard practice with increases and decreases.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
I have to agree with my colleague from Vegreville. It falls in the category of flim-flam. It is the opposite to the truth. If a legal expert reads the documents put out with the budget papers, the notice of ways and means motion and so on, he can come to only one conclusion. I quote from the budget papers:
The new rate will apply to sales by manufacturers and licensed wholesalers on goods sold or delivered to the purchaser, and on goods imported into Canada or taken out of warehouse for consumption, after November 16, 1978.
It is plain and simple. It says everything. However, we find later that it does not apply to sales by manufacturers to dealers after November 16. We have been talking about car dealerships. A car dealership is classed as a licensed wholesaler. Any car dealer would have no difficulty in concluding that it would apply to sales made after that date.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: By the manufacturer.
By the manufacturer and licensed wholesaler. I am talking about dealers generally.
You are always wrong.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: The minister says I am never on the side of wrong. That is the distinction. I want to hear the parliamentary secretary explain himself out of this. There has been some great confusion. The parliamentary secretary cannot dispute that on the basis of the volume of mail received by members of parliament regarding this provision. I know there are many dealers in his constituency who are very upset about this provision. I am sure if at all possible the parliamentary secretary would vote for the amendment put forward by my colleague from Vegreville.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I believe the hon. member for Saskatoon-Big-gar is quoting from page 22 of the document "Notice of Ways and Means Motions". It is important to read the two paragraphs that pertain. The hon. member is referring to sales by manufacturers, and yet the problem that was raised earlier by the hon. member for Vegreville and others relates to the problem faced by retailers. The paragraph from which the hon. member was quoting reads:
The new rate will apply to sales by manufacturers and licensed wholesalers on goods sold or delivered to the purchaser, and on goods imported into Canada or taken out of warehouse of consumption, after November 16, 1978.

A further paragraph in that same section reads:
In accordance with standard practice, no claims will be entertained for refunds of tax in respect of inventories of goods on which the 12 per cent tax has already been paid.
I am sure the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar is aware that the tax becomes payable when the goods leave the manufacturer's shop. The tax has obviously been paid by retailers on the stock they have on hand. It is made abundantly clear there will be no consideration of a claim on their part covering those inventories on which a higher rate of tax has already been paid. That is clear as a bell to all of us. I am sure it will be clear to the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar as he applies his expertise and takes a closer look at it.

Mr. Chairman, I am in full support of the amendment moved by my colleague. I appreciate that it has been recognized as constitutional by the Chair. The parliamentary secretary made a statement that intrigued me, that it was according to usual or standard practice. I did not think this government was bound in any way by what is standard practice because, with regard to the operations of this House, it has departed so far from the standard practices and principles of the House that we hardly recognize them any more. I could explain that if I had the time.
Progress reported.

speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of providing one address with one postal code for all federal
Postal Code
government departments and agencies in the cities of Ottawa and Hull and in the National Capital Region, namely:
Department or agency,
National Capital Region,
Ottawa-Hull,

He said: Mr. Speaker, the contents of this motion might have been dealt with in another way, but I feel I have a duty to put this motion before the House to allow the government to consider the initiative referred to in the notice. There is no need to explain that a number of departments having moved to Hull, there seems to be some confusion within departments as to their postal addresses.
I attempted for a few years to awake departmental awareness to this, and it seems this was not one of their priorities. Confusion ensued and today, looking at the postal address of some federal department buildings, we find addresses such as Northern Affairs, Terrasses Chaudiere, Ottawa, Ontario with an Ottawa postal code. It is a well known fact, Mr. Speaker, that Terrasses Chaudiere are located in Hull, Quebec, rather than Ottawa, Ontario. The answer I got was that naturally the postal code was an Ontario one because, as you know, postal codes are allocated by provinces.
My point is, Mr. Speaker, that for 50 years the good citizens of my constituency, Hull area, have been waging an uphill fight since 1917 to get their fair share of the moneys spent within the National Capital Region. I do not say this to be critical. I simply want to emphasize the problem we are now facing to present a reoccurrence of such a situation in the future and to avoid offending people and municipalities within the National Captial Region.
I am well aware that this is a new development and that the bureaucracy has perhaps not had the time to get used to life on the other side of the river. However, I believe that the government could have shown more foresight and provided a single postal code for the National Capital Region. This could have included all municipalities within this area. As a matter of fact, its boundaries are described in a document which provides for the Act on the National Capital Commission. I believe that this would enhance the pride of people who live in the national capital and I also believe that it would reflect the sense of belonging to the National Capital Region of all those who live on both sides of the river. We must not forget that the Hull area has been part of the National Capital Region for a long time. I therefore believe that we are entitled to the same privileges.
I know that it may be because of a historical accident that Ottawa was chosen by Queen Victoria in 1857 to be the capital of Canada. We must however recognize, as the premiers did in 1969 in Toronto, that the region of the national capital on both sides of the river makes up the real national capital of Canada. It is with this in mind, Mr. COMMONS DEBATES
March 23, 1979
Postal Code
Speaker, that I ask the House to agree to this motion, which I am sure does not call for a lot of speeches and which would please people on both sides of the river.
Some may object to this and say: Of course, the postal code is an Ontario postal code and Ottawa is in Ontario. I know all that. However, I do not like the idea of an Ontario postal code being used on the Quebec side for federal departments because the federal government, Mr. Speaker, does not belong any more to the people of Ontario than to the people of Quebec.
The federal government represents Canada as a whole and the National Capital Region is supposed to represent what Canada should represent. This is why Queen Victoria, when she chose the Ottawa area as the capital of the Province of Canada, as it was called at the time, because of its central position, between Upper and Lower Canada, and because it reflected the two major ethnic groups of that new country. Furthermore, the policy of the government has always been to encourage acceptance by every Canadian of the whole area as the capital of the country. This is my request, Mr. Speaker. I know that hon. members will support everything that is done in the National Capital Region, as they did for many years. I think that if we do not do this simple thing, it might create some problems which we would not like to discuss. I think that it is an administrative issue and that it can be easily done since the National Capital Region is unique. Not only is it unique in Canada, but considering everything that has been accomplished in the capital and that have been paid for by all Canadians, it reflects the origin and the spirit of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I also wish to draw your attention to some anomalies in the National Capital Region which might be corrected very simply. I refer particularly to various administrative decisions that approach stupidity. For instance, when I heard recently about the moving of the manpower centre in Place du Portage. That Manpower Centre would be moved elsewhere, in the new city core, on St. Joseph Boulevard, but the building not being completely finished it would be moved temporarily in some sort of dead-end in the building on Fontaine Street where traffic is very light, where people normally going to work do not have to go by, basically very far from any traffic.
I think the Manpower Centre should be located in the heart of the city where people pass by or can go in every day as in the case of all other large Manpower Centres in Canada. I find that disastrously stupid and I say that in this case at the Manpower Centre the decision is made by Montreal because being in the province of Quebec even if you see parliament and the federal buildings every day, Montreal is the place where the decisions are made in this case, namely the Manpower Centre.
I hope we can make the civil servants taking those decisions aware of that so as not to cause any prejudice to the people in the National Capital Region.
I think we have suffered enough for years and are still suffering from overgovernment, we are suffering enough from overtaxation, I hope that federal government through its bureaucracy by the means we can use will stop causing us prejudices, at least we will have a few prejudices less to suffer. I also heard all sorts of rumours, Mr. Speaker. I am told the Government Printing Office is being abolished. I find it quite odd that the printing of the debates and everything that comes under the House of Commons should be done here in Ottawa on Wellington Street in the Metropolitan building.
So I do not understand why things like that are done as that is taking away employees from the Government Printing Office itself. They are being brought on Ottawa's side and the others are told: In a few years, you will not have much to do because parliament as such will take over the distribution and the printing of its material.
In my opinion, the Canadian Government Printing Office certainly has specific functions to fulfil. One of those is undoubtedly to print what parliamentarians thrive on day after day, the literature with which hon. members provide us and the committee reports. I find it very funny that, living in the National Capital Region, we often find that decisions seem to have been taken without consulting one department or another. It might be a good idea to be more orderly to avoid causing any detriment to anyone. The postal code is one of those. It would be so easy to reach an agreement with the provinces of Quebec and Ontario on a new form of postal code which would satisfy everyone.
If Ottawa is displeased that its name is linked to Hull, and if Hull is displeased that its name is linked to Ottawa, we can easily find a compromise and speak of the National Capital Region of Canada. It would be much simpler to have a distinct code which would be neither a Quebec nor an Ontario code, but a special code for buildings located within the National Capital Region. This would extend beyond Hull to other municipalities, towns and cities where federal government buildings are located.
I think I have summarized briefly what I wanted to say. I felt it my duty to bring this important matter to the attention of the House and urge our leaders to act through the bureaucracy. We often do not have much to say in the way the bureaucracy does things because, as the saying goes, members of parliament move on, the bureaucracy remains. We sometime have the feeling that some people spend their time seeking solutions to simple problems and, in the process, complicate them to an extraordinary degree. That is therefore why, in the name of simplicity, in the name of Canadian unity, and in the name of all my constituents in the national capital, I urge hon. members to provide a greater degree of autonomy because this is the beginning of something bigger.

March 23, 1979

Mr. Speaker, the National Capital Region is in the process of losing all it has gained since 1867, for the simple reason that the powers of the federal government in the capital of Canada are very limited. If that trend continues, Parliament Hill will soon be just about the only place where the federal government will have a say. That, to my mind, is inconceivable because by building up the area on both sides of the river the federal government wanted specifically to develop a distinctive region where all Canadians might see the achievements of this country, in a given spot, from every point of view, whether it be culture, administration, museums or anything else. I am sure my hon. colleagues will avoid, by rejecting this motion, having all those small powers, that are ours and those of the federal government, disappear further. That is why by accepting this motion I am sure we will continue to keep or to indicate that we want to see the federal government keep a bit more autonomy, that autonomy which is now gradually being eroded, and those powers it was intended to have in 1867. I do not have to give a history lesson, however it was in 1857 that Queen Victoria decided to make Ottawa the capital of Canada. She did not say the capital of Canada but the capital of the Province of Canada which was the union of Upper Canada and Lower Canada, considering that Ottawa as such would have some powers, for example the same powers as the provinces because it was the capital of the Province of Canada. Some unforeseen historical events occurred, the Fathers of Confederation divided Canada into provinces and the capital of Canada was divided in two without any power, nor any jurisdiction over its development, over road construction or over education, because the Queen had indirectly given those powers to the capital of Canada at the time, except that it is reported in our history that apparently nobody ever realized it.
Postal Code
Anyhow, I think it was my duty to point out to this august assembly that anomaly which I hope will never occur again. Each and every one of us is proud of his or her identity, and I am sure that a member from one riding would not want to be mistaken for a member from another riding. We are proud of what we have, we are very proud to belong to the National Capital Region. Since 1917, the people from western Quebec have been very attached to the federal government, which has been our bread and butter and will continue to be so.
In view of all the reasons I mentioned, I trust that hon. members will quickly adopt this motion which will give the same identity to all those who live in the National Capital Region. And if it is adopted, we will be able to say, as some visitors have shouted from one side then the other: Long live the free capital region of Canada!
